source.title: Improving language models by retrieving from trillions of tokens
source.authors: Sebastian Borgeaud; Arthur Mensch; Jordan Hoffmann; Trevor Cai; Eliza Rutherford; Katie Millican; George van den Driessche; Jean-Baptiste Lespiau; Bogdan Damoc; Aidan Clark; D. de Las Casas; Aurelia Guy; Jacob Menick; Roman Ring; T. Hennigan; Saffron Huang; Lorenzo Maggiore; Chris Jones; Albin Cassirer; Andy Brock; Michela Paganini; Geoffrey Irving; O. Vinyals; Simon Osindero; K. Simonyan; Jack W. Rae; Erich Elsen; L. Sifre

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. There are minor text-extraction and layout artifacts, but the relevant sections and tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether architecture choices change held-out language-model loss, using ablations rather than the original scaling-law fitting method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports language-model results across model sizes and retrieval-database sizes, but does not fit or test a power law, test small-run extrapolation, or identify a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Those results therefore do not establish the scaling-law versions. The architecture ablations in Table 13 directly measure evaluation loss under altered model design choices. Scaling-law statements in the introduction and related work are contextual citations, not results from this study.
record.test_reason: RETRO cites Kaplan et al. as context and presents retrieval as complementary to parameter scaling. It fits no power law, tests no extrapolation and runs no fixed-compute allocation sweep. The Table 13 ablations vary components of its own retrieval method (cross-attention placement, encoder depth, query conditioning, embedding sharing) with parameter counts that change between variants. They are not depth/width shape tests of a language model at fixed parameter count, so they do not bear on V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly off. The main conclusion is that RETRO's retrieval gains do not diminish from 150M to 7B parameters and match non-retrieval models with about 10x more parameters on some datasets. The authors also find that gains grow with retrieval-database size, and that semi-parametric retrieval is an orthogonal, more efficient path than raw parameter scaling. The Table 13 ablations are an appendix check that the design choices are compute-efficient, not a headline conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates a retrieval-enhanced Transformer and architecture ablations using C4 evaluation bpb; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting or compute-allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: C4 loss changes with cross-attention placement; the authors also report small effects for query conditioning, positional encodings, embedding sharing, and encoder depth.

fits_no_version.finding: C4 eval bpb of RETRO improves as the evaluation-time retrieval database grows from 2B to 900B tokens (e.g. 7.5B model: 0.78 to 0.71). Gains are roughly constant across 172M–7.5B, said to equal about 10x parameters. No power law is fitted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss of retrieval-augmented LMs improves smoothly with retrieval-database size at evaluation time, and the gain from retrieval is constant across model scale.

record.problems: Architecture ablations use a single 247M parameter model and C4 evaluation; uncertainty estimates are not reported. The text does not state that variant parameter counts are matched.
record.rows_left_out: Language-model and downstream benchmark comparisons, retrieval-database-size sweeps, and other retrieval ablations are not rows because they do not test the scaling-law versions or the architecture-shape measure in V4.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss in parameters, tokens or compute. Baseline loss is reported at only 4 sizes (132M–7B), with no fit.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep. All models are trained on the same 419B tokens.
No depth/width/shape variation at fixed parameter count. The ablations concern retrieval components only.
No other modality or regime scaling law. Retrieval-database scaling is a different construct.
Downstream results (LAMBADA, NQ) are reported by size, but there is no test of predictability from scale or loss.
No comparison of exponents or fitting choices.

missing.what: Retrieval-free baseline C4 eval bpb at 132M/368M/1.3B/7.0B non-embedding parameters (0.98/0.92/0.84/0.78), all trained on 419B tokens, with no power-law fit. This is context only for V1, and four points over about 1.7 decades cannot establish the functional form.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 link is wrong. RETRO's ablations alter retrieval-specific components and change parameter counts, so they are not tests of 'shape matters little at fixed parameter count'. No row bears on any version, so no verdict labels are given.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit for held-out pretraining loss against parameters, training tokens, or compute; no test over several orders of magnitude with the other variables shown not to be bottlenecks.
No extrapolation from small-run fits to larger runs.
No fixed-compute sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
The ablations do not establish matched parameter counts across variants, vary width systematically, or test a broad range of architectures.
No other modalities or the stated repeated-data, fine-tuning, and transfer scaling-law regimes are tested.
Downstream results are reported, but the study does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss.
No comparison of scaling-law exponents or fitting choices, and no test of curves bending away from a power law.

rows.subject: 247M parameter Re t ro model
rows.stage_stated: trained on a compressed 157 billion token schedule for the ablation experiments
rows.operation_detail: Removed encoder conditioning on the previous chunk
rows.note: The paper describes query conditioning as providing a pure improvement; this variant has a small loss increase relative to default.
rows.check: Ablation of RETRO's own retrieval component (encoder query conditioning). This is not a depth/width/shape change at fixed parameter count and parameters are not matched, so it does not measure what V4 names.

rows.subject: 247M parameter Re t ro model
rows.stage_stated: trained on a compressed 157 billion token schedule for the ablation experiments
rows.operation_detail: Removed relative positional encodings in cross-attention
rows.note: The loss change is small; the paper reports that relative encodings improve training efficiency and performance.
rows.check: Ablation of the study's own method (relative positional encodings in cross-attention), not an architecture-shape test at fixed parameter count.

rows.subject: 247M parameter Re t ro model
rows.stage_stated: trained on a compressed 157 billion token schedule for the ablation experiments
rows.operation_detail: Shared encoder and decoder embedding matrices
rows.note: The paper states that sharing embeddings does not affect performance.
rows.check: Encoder/decoder embedding sharing changes parameter count and is a retrieval-method design choice, not a V4 shape test.

rows.subject: 247M parameter Re t ro model
rows.stage_stated: trained on a compressed 157 billion token schedule for the ablation experiments
rows.operation_detail: Used a 6-layer retrieval encoder rather than the default 2-layer encoder
rows.note: The paper describes this deeper encoder as producing a tiny loss decrease of 0.15% at a training-time cost of +20%.
rows.check: The 6-layer vs 2-layer retrieval encoder adds parameters (not fixed-N). It concerns the retrieval encoder, not the language model's depth/width shape.

rows.subject: 247M parameter Re t ro model
rows.stage_stated: trained on a compressed 157 billion token schedule for the ablation experiments
rows.operation_detail: Applied cross-attention only at the bottom layer
rows.note: The paper says attending only once at the top or bottom layer is a bad choice; the table gives this variant's evaluation loss.
rows.check: Cross-attention placement is a retrieval-method hyperparameter with parameter count varying across variants. The condition label also says 'top layer (1/12)', but the paper's text refers to the bottom layer.

rows.subject: 247M parameter Re t ro model
rows.stage_stated: trained on a compressed 157 billion token schedule for the ablation experiments
rows.operation_detail: Applied cross-attention only at a middle layer
rows.note: The paper describes attending once at a mid-depth layer as relatively sound.
rows.check: Cross-attention placement ablation of the study's own method, not a V4 shape test at fixed parameter count.

rows.subject: 247M parameter Re t ro model
rows.stage_stated: trained on a compressed 157 billion token schedule for the ablation experiments
rows.operation_detail: Applied cross-attention only at the top layer
rows.note: The paper says attending only once at the top or bottom layer is a bad choice.
rows.check: Cross-attention placement ablation of the study's own method, not a V4 shape test at fixed parameter count.

rows.subject: 247M parameter Re t ro model
rows.stage_stated: trained on a compressed 157 billion token schedule for the ablation experiments
rows.note: This variant has a substantially higher loss than the default; the paper characterizes its design choice as less efficient.
rows.check: Cross-attention at all layers adds many parameters, so it is not fixed-N. It is a retrieval-method ablation, and the 'partial' state against V4 is not meaningful.

rows.subject: 247M parameter Re t ro model
rows.stage_stated: trained on a compressed 157 billion token schedule for the ablation experiments
rows.operation_detail: Applied cross-attention every third layer starting at layer one
rows.note: The loss is close to the default; the paper's default applies cross-attention every third layer starting at layer six.
rows.check: Cross-attention frequency/offset ablation of the study's own method, not a V4 shape test.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: No-query-conditioning, no-CA-positional-encoding, shared-embedding, deeper-encoder, mid-layer-only, and every-third-from-layer-one ablations
reader_labels.reason: Evaluation losses are close to the default value of 0.822 bpb in these ablations (R1–R6, R9), consistent with small effects for these tested choices.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Cross-attention placement, especially cross-attention at all layers
reader_labels.reason: Loss varies with placement, reaching 0.860 bpb when cross-attention is applied at all layers, while the authors describe top- or bottom-only placement as poor choices (R5, R7, R8).
